pages.name: UNIT 1 — What Is Phonics?
pages.subtitle: WHAT IS PHONICS?
pages.html:
Teaching Note
Phonics connects spoken sounds with written letters and patterns. In Grade 5 it helps readers approach long, unfamiliar and academic words.
Worked Example
For government or photosynthesis, look for familiar chunks, divide the word into manageable parts, sound them out, blend them and check the sentence.
Class Exercise
Name one long word from a school subject that used to look hard to you.
Explain in your own words what 'phonics' means at Grade 5 level.
Why might phonics still matter even though you can already read simple words?
Challenge
Choose an unfamiliar school word and describe how you would decode it.

pages.name: UNIT 1 — Why Phonics Matters
pages.subtitle: WHY PHONICS MATTERS
pages.html:
Why Phonics Matters
By Grade 5, phonics is less about sounding out short words and more about unlocking the long, academic vocabulary you meet in science, history and maths.
Worked Example
A reader who knows that photo- means 'light' and -graph means 'writing' can work out photograph, photography and photographer without being told each one.
Class Exercise
List two long words from a recent lesson (science, social studies, or maths) that you had to sound out.
Pick one of those words and break it into smaller chunks.
Explain how knowing the chunks helped you read the whole word.
Challenge
Find a word in your textbook with more than three syllables and explain how you decoded it.

pages.name: UNIT 1 — Decoding + Meaning
pages.subtitle: DECODING + MEANING
pages.html:
Decoding + Meaning: Word Parts
Many long words are built from smaller meaningful parts: a prefix (added to the front), a root (the core meaning) and a suffix (added to the end). Recognising these parts helps you decode AND understand the word at the same time.
Worked Example
un + happy + ness = unhappiness (not happy, and the state of it). re + view = review (to view again). bio (life) + graph (writing) + y = biography (writing about a life).

Challenge

pages.name: UNIT 1 — Fluency + Accuracy
pages.subtitle: FLUENCY + ACCURACY
pages.html:
Fluency + Accuracy
Fluent reading means recognising words automatically and reading with natural expression and phrasing, not word-by-word. Accuracy means decoding every word correctly, especially long or unfamiliar ones.
Worked Example
A fluent Grade 5 reader can read 'The extraordinary discovery amazed the entire community' smoothly, pausing at the comma and stressing 'extraordinary' and 'amazed' for meaning.
Class Exercise
Read the worked example sentence aloud twice, then a third time with more expression.
Circle the word in that sentence you found hardest to read smoothly.
Explain what made that word difficult: length, an unusual pattern, or an unfamiliar meaning?
Challenge
Time yourself reading the worked example sentence aloud. Try to read it again, faster and more smoothly, without losing accuracy.

pages.name: UNIT 1 — Reader's Strategy
pages.subtitle: READER'S STRATEGY
pages.html:
Reader's Strategy: The 4-Step Fix-Up
When you meet a hard word, use this strategy: 1) CHUNK it into recognisable parts, 2) BLEND the parts together, 3) CHECK it against the sentence for meaning, 4) REREAD the sentence smoothly.
Worked Example
government → chunk: govern + ment → blend: /guhv-ern-ment/ → check: does 'government' make sense running the country? → reread the sentence smoothly.

Class Exercise

Challenge

pages.name: UNIT 5 — Vocabulary Challenge

pages.subtitle: SENTENCE EDITING
pages.html:
Teaching Note
Sentence Editing: fix both a spelling error and a grammar error in each sentence.

Challenge

pages.name: UNIT 5 — Independent Word Study
pages.subtitle: INDEPENDENT WORD STUDY
pages.html:
Teaching Note
Independent Word Study: choose your own -ace word from the full family list to research.

Full family: necklace, palace, menace, solace, grimace, surface, preface, populace, terrace, furnace, embrace, disgrace.

Challenge

pages.subtitle: WEEKLY REVIEW
pages.html:

Weekly Review: cumulative check across the whole -ace family so far.

Recall: necklace, palace, menace, solace, grimace, surface, preface, populace, terrace, furnace, embrace, disgrace.

pages.name: UNIT 6 — Reading Fluency
pages.subtitle: READING FLUENCY
pages.html:
Teaching Note
Fluency means smooth, natural reading with expression rather than word by word.
Worked Example
courageous → divide into syllables → identify vowel sounds → sound each part → blend → check the sentence.
Class Exercise
Read the worked example word aloud three times, getting smoother each time.
Explain what 'expression' means when reading aloud.
Name one word you personally read more smoothly after practice.
Challenge
Explain how sentence punctuation (commas, full stops) should change how you pace your reading.

pages.name: UNIT 6 — Repeated Reading
pages.subtitle: REPEATED READING
pages.html:
Teaching Note
Repeated reading builds speed and smoothness: reading the same passage several times improves fluency.
Worked Example
Passage 1 will be read three times in the next lesson: once for accuracy, once for speed, once for expression.
Class Exercise
Predict which of your three future readings of Passage 1 will be your best, and why.
Explain the difference between reading for accuracy and reading for expression.

Challenge

pages.name: UNIT 6 — Accuracy Check
pages.subtitle: ACCURACY CHECK
pages.html:
Teaching Note
Accuracy check: count the words you misread and identify the pattern behind each mistake.
Worked Example
If you misread 'exhausted' as 'exhousted', the mistake is in the vowel team, not the consonants.
Class Exercise
Read Passage 3 (next page) once and mark any word you misread.
For each error, name the specific pattern that caused it (vowel team, silent letter, stress, etc).
Reread the same sentence correctly after identifying your error.
Challenge
Explain why naming the exact reason for a misread word helps you avoid repeating it.

pages.name: UNIT 6 — Expression
pages.subtitle: EXPRESSION
pages.html:
Teaching Note
Expression means using your voice to show meaning: pausing at commas, raising pitch for questions, and stressing important words.
Worked Example
"He remembered his coach's advice: focus on the next step, not the whole distance." — notice the colon and comma control the pacing.
Class Exercise
Read the worked example sentence aloud, pausing exactly at the colon and comma.
Choose one sentence from Passage 1 and mark where you would pause.
Read your chosen sentence aloud with expression.
Challenge
Explain how reading with no expression at all changes how a listener understands a passage.

pages.name: UNIT 6 — Fluency Passage 1
pages.subtitle: FLUENCY PASSAGE 1
pages.html:
The village was quiet at dawn. A gentle breeze moved through the old wooden bridge, and somewhere in the distance a dog began to bark. Mariam walked slowly along the path, listening to the birds calling from the tall trees. She noticed the market stalls being set up for the day, and the smell of fresh bread drifted from the bakery. By the time the sun rose fully over the hills, the whole village had come alive with voices, laughter, and the steady rhythm of morning work.

Deep beneath the ocean's surface, a hidden world thrives in complete darkness. Strange creatures glow with their own light, guiding them through the icy water. Some fish have enormous eyes that capture the smallest traces of light, while others sense vibrations instead of seeing at all. Scientists who study this environment use special submarines to explore places no human has ever reached. Every expedition uncovers new species, reminding us that our planet still holds countless mysteries waiting to be discovered.

pages.name: UNIT 6 — Fluency Passage 3
pages.subtitle: FLUENCY PASSAGE 3
pages.html:
Kwame had never run more than a mile before, but today he stood at the starting line of the district race, determined to finish. His legs felt heavy after the first few minutes, and his breathing grew ragged as the hill ahead seemed to stretch on forever. He remembered his coach's advice: focus on the next step, not the whole distance. Slowly, he found his rhythm again, pushing past the ache in his muscles. When he finally crossed the finish line, exhausted but smiling, he realized that courage was not about feeling strong, it was about continuing anyway.

pages.name: UNIT 6 — Proving a Word

Proving a word means using letter sounds AND sentence meaning together to confirm you read it correctly.
